claim: For flexible-joint robots, a cascaded architecture combining inner joint-torque feedback with an outer impedance controller can retain the physical joint elasticity while reducing the apparent motor inertia and enabling passivity-based stability analysis. The first proposed controller separately implements motor-position stiffness/damping and quasi-static gravity compensation, whereas the second merges gravity compensation with stiffness design to satisfy the desired static stiffness relation exactly. These guarantees are conditional on the reduced flexible-joint model, positive-definiteness and potential-curvature assumptions, and free-motion or passive-environment conditions; DLR experiments support impact and model-error robustness empirically but do not establish unconditional global stability or exact dynamic impedance realization.
claim_locator: Abstract; Sections II–IV on the design idea, reduced flexible-joint model, torque-feedback interpretation, and gravity-potential assumptions; Section V, especially Eqs. 8–23 and Propositions 1–2; Section VI, especially Eqs. 34–47 and Propositions 3–4; Section VII Cartesian extension and Proposition 5; Section VIII and Figs. 6–13; Section IX summary.
epistemic_status: Full-text primary control-theory and experimental study. Stability and passivity statements are theorem-supported only under their stated assumptions; hardware behavior is author-reported and was not independently reproduced.
problem_and_setting: Classical rigid-joint impedance controllers do not adequately address the fourth-order dynamics and oscillations introduced by elastic transmissions. The paper considers robots whose motor and link coordinates are separated by compliant joints and seeks a desired stiffness-and-damping relation to external forces while leaving link-side inertia unchanged. The practical setting is torque-sensor-equipped DLR lightweight robots intended for compliant interaction and contact with unknown or passive environments.
method_or_mechanism: Both controllers use a cascade. The inner loop negatively feeds back measured joint torque and algebraically transforms the motor equation so that the original diagonal motor inertia B behaves as a selected smaller positive-definite apparent inertia Bθ. This does not make the torque-feedback controller itself passive; rather, the controlled motor dynamics together with torque feedback form a passive block that can be interconnected with the passive link-side dynamics. The first outer controller splits its input into a motor-position PD term and a motor-position-based quasi-static gravity compensation term. Its stiffness gain accounts for the series connection of controller stiffness and physical joint stiffness, and its gravity estimate is obtained from the inverse of the static motor-to-link mapping. The second controller defines l(q)=g(q)−Kθ(q−qd), constructs the corresponding inverse quasi-static mapping, and combines gravity and stiffness in a single potential-based term plus damping. This merged design enforces Kθ(q0−qd)=τext exactly at steady state for constant external torque. Neither controller can reduce the complete fourth-order flexible-joint dynamics to the desired second-order impedance exactly; higher inner-loop torque feedback only improves the approximation.
content_summary: The paper formulates a reduced flexible-joint model with link inertia, Coriolis and centrifugal terms, gravity, diagonal linear joint stiffness, diagonal motor inertia, motor angles, link angles, and external link torques. Negative joint-torque feedback is interpreted physically as reducing apparent motor inertia, improving approximation of the desired impedance and damping elastic-joint oscillations without shaping link-side inertia. For the first controller, stiffness/damping and gravity compensation are designed separately. Its passivity proof decomposes the closed loop into passive motor-side and link-side subsystems, while Proposition 2 proves asymptotic stability in free motion under Assumptions 1 and 2 and global asymptotic stability only when the gravity-curvature bound holds globally. The separate construction is stable and allows desired positive-definite stiffness arbitrarily close to zero, but it does not generally realize the desired static stiffness relation exactly when gravity and nonzero external torque act together. The second controller merges gravity and compliance through a combined potential. Proposition 4 proves free-motion asymptotic stability under Assumption 3, global asymptotic stability when that assumption holds globally, and passivity from external torque to link velocity during interaction. It exactly realizes the specified static stiffness relation, while still only approximating the full desired dynamic impedance. The Cartesian extension adds restrictions from Jacobian singularities and redundancy: damping is positive definite only away from singularity, nonredundant stability is local, and redundant robots require additional nullspace behavior. Experiments used the Cartesian extension on seven-degree-of-freedom DLR Lightweight Robot II and III platforms. Human push-pull tests produced force-displacement behavior close to the desired low and high Cartesian stiffnesses. In a wooden-surface impact test, the system remained stable, a measured static stiffness of about 3882 N/m was close to the commanded 4000 N/m, and the authors report that high impact velocities were handled. Step-response tests with a known approximately 4.5 kg load showed response changes expected from leaving effective inertia unshaped. In a load-model-error test, the same load was removed from gravity compensation at 0.26 s; position accuracy degraded by an offset consistent with the commanded 2000 N/m stiffness, while the system remained stable in the reported trial.
synthesis_role: Foundational conditional-stability card in the evolution of impedance control from rigid-joint PD behavior toward torque-sensor-based, passivity-grounded control of elastic-joint robots. It explains how inner torque feedback can improve dynamic performance without discarding joint elasticity and how potential-based gravity/stiffness design separates dynamic approximation from exact static compliance.
development_link: The work extends impedance control to flexible-joint robots by embedding a fast torque-feedback loop inside a slower impedance structure and interpreting that feedback through apparent motor-inertia scaling. The first controller establishes a passivity-compatible decomposition but exposes a static accuracy limitation when gravity and compliance are designed separately. The second controller resolves that specific limitation by merging the corresponding potentials, obtaining exact steady-state stiffness under constant load. The progression improves conditional stability, contact robustness, and static accuracy while retaining constraints from unshaped link inertia, physical joint stiffness, gravity-potential curvature, Jacobian singularities, and model-dependent gravity compensation.

evidence.statement: Negative joint-torque feedback transforms the motor dynamics from inertia B to a selectable apparent inertia Bθ, so increasing torque-feedback gain makes the closed-loop response approximate the desired impedance more closely and damps elastic-joint torque oscillations.
evidence.support_scope: Sections II–III, Eqs. 3–5, and simulation in Figs. 4–5.

evidence.statement: The first controller uses a motor-position PD term for compliance and a separate motor-position-based quasi-static gravity-compensation term derived through an inverse static mapping.

Under Assumptions 1 and 2, the first controller is asymptotically stable in free motion; it is globally asymptotically stable only if Assumption 1 holds globally, meaning Qp=Rn in the paper's formulation.

The first controller's closed loop is represented as an interconnection of passive subsystems; the passivity analysis additionally assumes a globally bounded gravity potential, as for robots with rotational joints only.
The first controller does not guarantee the exact desired static relation under simultaneous gravity and nonzero external torque because stiffness and gravity compensation are designed separately.
The second controller combines gravity compensation and desired stiffness through l(q)=g(q)−Kθ(q−qd) and enforces Kθ(q0−qd)=τext exactly at steady state.
evidence.support_scope: Section VI-A and VI-C, Eqs. 34–45 and steady-state derivation.

evidence.statement: Under Assumption 3, the second controller is asymptotically stable in free motion; global asymptotic stability requires Assumption 3 globally, and interaction is passive as a mapping from external torque to link velocity.

The Cartesian extension is passive, but local asymptotic stability is established only for the nonredundant, nonsingular case; redundant robots require nullspace control and Jacobian singularities obstruct a global result.
evidence.support_scope: Section VII-B and discussion following Eq. 59.

evidence.statement: On DLR Lightweight Robot II, measured force-displacement behavior matched the commanded low and high Cartesian compliance reasonably well, and an impact against a wooden passive surface remained stable with measured static stiffness about 3882 N/m versus 4000 N/m commanded.
evidence.support_scope: Section VIII, Figs. 7–11 and Tables I–II.

evidence.statement: On DLR Lightweight Robot III, an approximately 4.5 kg end-effector load altered the step response as expected because effective inertia was not shaped.
evidence.support_scope: Section VIII, Fig. 12 and Table III.

evidence.statement: When the approximately 4.5 kg load was removed from the controller's gravity model at 0.26 s, the reported position offset followed the commanded 2000 N/m compliance while the hardware remained stable.
The force-torque sensor mounted at the end effector was used only for experimental evaluation, while implementation relied on motor-position and joint-torque sensing.

evidence_kind: Analytical controller derivation, contraction-mapping results, storage-function passivity analysis, Lyapunov and LaSalle asymptotic-stability proofs, supporting simulation, and author-reported DLR hardware experiments involving compliance, impact, known payload, and gravity-model error.
boundary_conditions: The base analysis assumes Spong's reduced flexible-joint model with linear elastic joints, diagonal physical joint stiffness K, diagonal motor inertia B, ideal motor torque sources, and initially no transmission damping; visco-elastic joints are addressed as an extension.
The link inertia M(q) must be symmetric positive definite, and the standard skew-symmetry energy property of Ṁ−2C is required.

The torque-feedback interpretation requires a selected apparent motor inertia Bθ that remains positive definite; claimed robustness to inertia-parameter errors requires inertia matrices to remain positive definite and B to remain diagonal.

The design shapes stiffness and damping but deliberately leaves link-side inertia unchanged; it cannot realize an arbitrary second-order mass-spring-damper impedance exactly for the fourth-order flexible-joint system.

Assumption 1 requires the gravity-potential Hessian, normalized by physical joint stiffness, to have supremum below one; physically, joint stiffness must be sufficient to support the robot against its own weight.

Assumption 2 requires desired joint stiffness Kθ to be symmetric positive definite and compatible with a positive-definite controller stiffness arising from its series connection with physical joint stiffness; desired stiffness cannot exceed the relevant physical joint-stiffness bound.

The first controller's passivity proof assumes a gravity potential bounded over the considered configuration domain; the asymptotic-stability proof does not require that additional bounded-potential condition but still requires Assumptions 1 and 2.

Proposition 2 applies to free motion with zero external torque. Its global conclusion requires the gravity-curvature assumption over all configurations; otherwise the result is limited to the admissible domain Qp.

The first controller can choose positive-definite desired stiffness arbitrarily close to zero without an additional gravity-induced lower bound, but zero or indefinite stiffness is outside the stated theorem.

Assumption 3 for the second controller bounds the Hessian of the combined gravity-and-stiffness potential and implicitly imposes an upper bound on desired stiffness relative to physical joint stiffness.
Proposition 4 establishes free-motion asymptotic stability and interaction passivity under Assumption 3; global asymptotic stability requires that assumption globally.
Static exactness of the second controller concerns constant external torque and equilibrium, not exact transient realization of the target dynamic impedance.
The inverse quasi-static maps are assumed exact in the analysis, whereas implementation approximates them iteratively; the authors report one or two iterations as practically satisfactory.
For robots with prismatic joints or restricted workspaces, global contraction is not automatic; the iterations must remain within a region where the normalized Hessian bound holds.

Cartesian damping is positive definite only where the Jacobian has suitable rank. Jacobian singularities restrict the region of attraction, and redundant robots need additional nullspace control for asymptotic stability.
The Cartesian experiments validate a particular seven-degree-of-freedom DLR implementation and do not by themselves verify the full joint-space global theorem.
The impact result assumes contact with a passive wooden environment and cannot be generalized to arbitrary active, time-varying, or nonpassive contacts.

The large gravity-model-error result is a single author-reported hardware experiment; it separates observed stability from degraded equilibrium accuracy but does not prove robustness to arbitrary gravity errors, payloads, or configurations.
Experimental force sensing at the end effector was for evaluation only; controller operation still requires joint-torque measurement, either directly or indirectly through link-position sensing.
assumptions: The Controller-registered extracted text faithfully represents the paper despite character-encoding artifacts in mathematical symbols.
Bθ denotes the positive-definite scaled apparent motor inertia produced by the inner torque-feedback law.

The phrase 'desired stiffness smaller than physical joint stiffness' summarizes the positive-definiteness and Hessian bounds in the relevant joint-stiffness metric rather than asserting a scalar inequality for every possible coupled design.
The theorem-supported claims are interpreted only for the paper's model and exact analytical controller, not for arbitrary discretized, saturated, delayed, or noisy implementations.
The experimental statement that stability was maintained under load-model error is treated as an observation consistent with passivity arguments, not as a new general theorem.
The reported impact robustness is attributed jointly to the cascaded controller, mechanical compliance, and a passive environment; causality is not isolated experimentally.
The target impedance is understood as desired stiffness and damping with unchanged link-side inertia, not full inertia shaping.

reported: A straightforward rigid-joint impedance controller applied to a flexible-joint robot gives unsatisfactory oscillation damping and positioning performance.
Without torque feedback, simulation showed higher-frequency oscillations and large overshoot; reducing apparent motor inertia damped these oscillations.
The first controller does not satisfy the desired static stiffness relation exactly for general nonzero external torque in gravity because stiffness and gravity compensation are separated.
Neither proposed controller exactly realizes the target second-order dynamic impedance of the fourth-order flexible-joint system.
Cartesian global stability is obstructed by Jacobian singularities, and redundant Cartesian control requires an additional nullspace behavior.
With an approximately 4.5 kg load omitted from the gravity model, equilibrium position accuracy degraded even though the reported hardware trial remained stable.
The inverse quasi-static mappings generally cannot be computed directly and are approximated iteratively in practice.
inferred: Sensor noise limits how far apparent motor inertia can be reduced through torque-feedback gain, creating a practical performance-versus-noise boundary.

Unmodeled actuator dynamics, saturation, delay, friction, nonlinear elasticity, or inaccurate torque sensing could violate the idealized passivity and stability conditions even when the continuous-time theorem assumptions hold nominally.

The observed survival of one large gravity-compensation error demonstrates empirical robustness but not arbitrary-model-error stability; gravity errors can shift the equilibrium and may invalidate regional potential assumptions in other configurations.
Exact static stiffness does not imply accurate transient impedance because motor and link inertias remain in the fourth-order dynamics.
Passivity with a passive environment does not guarantee equivalent behavior against active or nonpassive contacts.
Global joint-space results do not transfer automatically to the experimental redundant Cartesian controller, whose stability is local and requires additional nullspace treatment.
Very low desired stiffness may satisfy the first controller's theorem but can permit large deflections and reduced task accuracy even while stability is preserved.
